stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the urgent care clinic because of a sudden onset of painless gross hematuria. He has no history of fever, dysuria, or flank pain. He recently returned from a high-altitude hiking trip in the Andes mountains. His medical history is unremarkable, and he takes no medications. Vitals are: temperature 36.6°C, pulse 78/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 14.5 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 88 fL. A urinalysis reveals 2+ blood and no white blood cells or nitrites. Renal ultrasound shows increased echogenicity of the renal medullae bilaterally.
lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The patient presents with painless gross hematuria and renal medullary echogenicity following a trigger of high altitude (low oxygen tension). This is characteristic of renal papillary necrosis (RPN) seen in patients with sickle cell trait (SCT). In SCT, individuals are typically asymptomatic and have normal hemoglobin levels, but the low pO2 and acidic pH of the renal medulla promote sickling of red blood cells, leading to microvascular ischemia and sloughing of the renal papillae. IgA nephropathy typically presents with hematuria following a respiratory infection. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis presents with hematuria, hypertension, and edema following a pharyngeal or skin infection. Analgesic nephropathy is caused by chronic NSAID abuse and also causes RPN, but this patient has no history of such use. A urinary tract infection would typically be associated with dysuria and positive nitrites/leukocyte esterase.
teaching_point: Sickle cell trait can cause renal papillary necrosis due to sickling in the low-oxygen environment of the renal medulla, often triggered by extreme physiologic stress such as high altitude.

distractor_rationale.A: Causes RPN, but is associated with chronic NSAID or acetaminophen use, not high-altitude exposure.
distractor_rationale.B: Presents as episodic hematuria usually triggered by upper respiratory infections.
distractor_rationale.C: Presents with hematuria, edema, and hypertension after a streptococcal infection.
distractor_rationale.D: Correct: Triggered by hypoxia in the renal medulla in patients with HbAS.
distractor_rationale.E: Presents with dysuria and positive urinalysis for nitrites/leukocytes.
